questions.question: How is CSS selector specificity calculated?
questions.title: Calculating CSS selector specificity
questions.direct_answer: Specificity is compared as an ordered tuple: IDs; then classes, attributes, and pseudo-classes; then type selectors and pseudo-elements. The universal selector adds nothing, and a larger earlier component wins before later components are considered.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can calculate and compare real selectors without treating the tuple as a base-ten number.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding the tuple into one score or including combinators and the universal selector.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Calculate examples and distinguish specificity from the earlier cascade steps.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Specificity compares ID, class-like, and type-like counts in order.
Attributes and pseudo-classes count with classes.
Combinators and the universal selector add no specificity.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Selector specificity is an ordered three-part weight. The first number counts ID selectors, the second counts classes, attributes, and pseudo-classes, and the third counts type selectors and pseudo-elements. Comparison begins at the first number and moves right only when tied.

For example, `#app .card h2::before` has one ID, one class, and two type-like selectors, so its tuple is 1-1-2. `.page .card.featured h2` is 0-3-1. The first selector wins on specificity because one ID beats any number in the later components.

Combinators such as `>` and `+`, the universal selector `*`, and `:where()` add no weight. Functional selectors need their own rule: `:is()`, `:not()`, and `:has()` use the most specific selector in their argument list.

Specificity is not the first or only cascade decision. A declaration in a winning origin, importance level, or cascade layer can beat a more specific declaration in a lower-precedence group. Source order settles the conflict only after the earlier criteria and specificity tie.

I calculate specificity when debugging, but I design stylesheets around low, predictable selectors. A component class is usually clearer than an ID-heavy chain, and cascade layers can express architectural priority without continually making selectors stronger.

sections.title: Compare tuples from left to right
sections.content: Do not convert 1-0-0 and 0-20-0 into decimal scores. The tuple is lexicographic: any non-zero ID component wins over a selector with no IDs, regardless of how many classes the second selector contains.

sections.title: Inline styles belong to a separate cascade step
sections.content: Tutorials sometimes write specificity with an extra inline-style column. The current cascade specification handles element-attached style declarations as a precedence step before selector specificity is compared. For everyday debugging, the practical result is still that a normal style attribute beats a normal author style rule in the same context, but treating it as an ID selector hides the real cascade model.

sections.title: Count each selector component
sections.content:
| Selector | IDs | Classes / attributes / pseudo-classes | Types / pseudo-elements |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| #app .card h2::before | 1 | 1 | 2 |
| .page .card.featured h2 | 0 | 3 | 1 |
| :where(main) .card | 0 | 1 | 0 |

questions.question: In what order does the CSS cascade resolve conflicting declarations?
questions.title: The CSS cascade sorting order
questions.direct_answer: For declarations that apply to the same element and property, the cascade compares origin and importance, encapsulation context, element-attached styles, cascade layers, specificity, scope proximity where applicable, and finally order of appearance. Specificity matters only after the earlier categories tie.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner knows why a more specific rule can still lose.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reducing the cascade to specificity plus last rule wins.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Place layers and important declarations correctly and use DevTools to identify the winning step.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Only matching, valid declarations enter the cascade.
Origin and importance are considered before author specificity.
Cascade-layer order is considered before specificity within an origin.
Later source order wins only when all earlier criteria tie.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The cascade resolves one property on one element at a time. It first filters to declarations whose stylesheet applies, whose condition is true, whose selector matches, and whose syntax is valid. It then sorts that candidate list by precedence.

Origin and importance come before normal author specificity. User-agent, user, author, animation, and transition values occupy defined levels, and important declarations reverse some normal origin and layer priorities so user accessibility overrides can remain powerful.

Within the same origin and context, cascade layers express an explicit order. For normal author rules, an unlayered rule comes after named layers and beats them even with a weaker selector. Inside the same winning layer, specificity is compared; if that also ties, later appearance wins.

For example, a highly specific framework rule placed in an early `framework` layer can lose to a simple `.button` rule in a later `components` layer. That is intentional architectural priority, not a specificity bug.

When debugging, I inspect the computed property in DevTools and find the first precedence category where the candidates differ. This is faster and more accurate than adding selectors or `!important`, and it keeps the cascade understandable for the next change.

sections.title: Specificity is one checkpoint, not the whole cascade
sections.content: A declaration cannot use high specificity to jump out of a lower origin, importance group, or normal cascade layer. Only declarations that survive the earlier sorting criteria are compared by selector weight. Equal weight then reaches scope proximity where supported and source order.

sections.title: Important layer order is deliberately reversed
sections.content: For normal declarations, later layers have greater priority, with unlayered author styles after named layers. For important declarations, earlier layers win. This reversal protects foundational important rules from being casually overridden later and mirrors the accessibility purpose of important origin ordering. It is another reason to reserve `!important` for deliberate guarantees rather than routine component styling.

sections.title: A practical conflict-resolution path
sections.content: valid + matching? → origin / importance → context / attached style → layer order → specificity → scope proximity → source order → winning value

sections.title: Let layer order beat selector strength

questions.question: How do cascade layers help control CSS specificity?
questions.title: Managing priority with cascade layers
questions.direct_answer: Cascade layers let authors declare priority between groups such as reset, framework, base, components, and utilities. Because layer order is evaluated before selector specificity, a later normal layer can override an earlier one without stronger selector chains.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner understands layers as explicit cascade priority rather than namespaces.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming the most specific selector still wins across normal layers or overlooking unlayered rules.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Declare layer order once and explain the reversed rule for important declarations.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: @layer establishes ordered groups inside a cascade origin.
Later named layers win for normal declarations.
Unlayered normal author rules outrank named layers.
Important declarations reverse the layer priority.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Cascade layers provide an architectural priority system for styles from the same origin. A project can declare `@layer reset, vendor, base, components, utilities` once, then place rules into those groups even when their files are loaded from different locations.

For normal declarations, a later layer wins over an earlier layer before selector specificity is considered. A small utility selector can therefore override a deeply nested vendor selector when the utility layer intentionally has higher priority.

For example, a date-picker package can be imported into a `vendor` layer and local component corrections can live in `components`. The local class no longer needs to copy the package's long selector or use `!important` merely to win.

Unlayered normal author rules have higher priority than every named author layer, so accidentally leaving a file unlayered can defeat the architecture. Important declarations reverse layer order; the earliest important layer has priority, which lets a foundation layer protect deliberate guarantees.

Layers do not replace good selectors, scoping, or component ownership. They solve priority between groups. I declare their order near the stylesheet entry point and keep ordinary component selectors low so both the architecture and individual rules remain easy to reason about.

sections.title: Priority belongs to concerns, not selector length
sections.content: Without layers, teams often make selectors increasingly specific to override third-party or older styles. Layers state which concern should win first. Specificity then resolves conflicts only among declarations inside the same winning layer.

sections.title: First declaration fixes a layer's position
sections.content: A statement such as `@layer reset, vendor, components, utilities;` establishes order before content is loaded. Later blocks with those names add rules to the existing positions; they do not move the layers. This is especially useful for imports because code-splitting or file order no longer silently changes the intended priority. Keep truly unlayered styles intentional because their normal declarations sit after the named layers.

sections.title: Normal author-layer priority
sections.content:
lower priority                                      higher priority
reset → vendor → base → components → utilities → unlayered rules
          specificity is compared only inside the winning layer

sections.title: Override a vendor rule without a selector race

questions.question: How do you debug a CSS rule that is not applying?
questions.title: Debugging a losing CSS declaration
questions.direct_answer: Inspect the element's computed property, confirm the selector matches and the declaration is valid, then compare the winning and losing rules by cascade origin, importance, layer, specificity, and source order. Fix the earliest real cause instead of immediately adding !important.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner has a repeatable debugging process grounded in the cascade.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Appending !important or a longer selector before checking that the property is valid and applicable.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Separate a crossed-out declaration, an invalid value, inheritance, and layout behaviour.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Confirm the selector matches the intended element.
Check that the property name and value are valid and applicable.
Inspect the computed property and its winning declaration.
Compare layer, specificity, and source order before changing code.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I first select the exact element in browser DevTools and find the property in the Computed panel. That shows the final value and usually links back to the winning declaration. In the Rules panel, a crossed-out value means another candidate won, while an ignored or warning-marked value may be invalid.

I then confirm the selector actually matches and that the property applies to this element and layout mode. For example, `justify-content` will not arrange children until the element establishes a compatible flex or grid formatting context.

If two valid declarations conflict, I compare the cascade in order: origin and importance, layer, specificity, then source order when the earlier factors tie. For example, a simple unlayered rule can beat a highly specific rule inside a named layer.

I also check inheritance and shorthand resets. A later `background` shorthand can reset an earlier `background-color`, and a child may inherit color from a nearer ancestor than expected. State classes, media queries, and unsupported conditions can explain why a rule appears only at certain widths or interactions.

The fix should express intent: correct the selector, move the concern to the proper layer, remove an accidental shorthand, or set the missing layout context. `!important` is a last deliberate guarantee, not a diagnostic tool, because it hides rather than explains ordinary priority.

sections.title: Find where the declaration leaves the pipeline
sections.content: A rule can fail before the cascade because it does not match, its condition is false, or its declaration is invalid. It can lose inside the cascade, or it can win yet appear ineffective because the property does not apply in the current layout. DevTools separates those cases.

sections.title: Computed value and visible result are not always the same question
sections.content: A property may have the expected computed value while another rendering rule prevents the expected appearance. `z-index: 9999` can be trapped in a lower stacking context, a transformed element can create a new context, and an opaque overlay can cover a correctly colored element. After confirming the cascade winner, inspect layout, stacking, and box geometry rather than making the selector stronger.

sections.title: A targeted debugging decision
sections.content:
selector matches? → declaration valid? → property applies? → declaration wins cascade? → layout/paint shows it?
      no: fix target     no: fix value      no: add context      no: compare rules      no: inspect geometry

sections.title: Find the missing layout context
sections.content:
```html
``` justify-content was valid but had no intended flex alignment until display: flex established the context.
